source_policy.primary_preference: Use official government, intergovernmental, regulatory, scientific-journal and securities-filings sources for factual claims.
source_policy.attribution_rule: Corporate and advocacy claims must remain attributed and must not be presented as independent findings.
source_policy.freshness_rule: Current permit, negotiation and trial status must be rechecked immediately before script lock.

sources.publisher: Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology (JAMSTEC)
sources.title: Results of the rare-earth-mud mining-system connection test in the Minamitorishima EEZ
supports: Continuous lifting of rare-earth mud from a pipe depth of 5,569 metres
Recovery from three rare-earth layers during a three-day test
Planned approximately one-month production-chain trial beginning February 2027
Integrated industrial and economic assessment targeted by March 2028
sources.limitation: Confirms technical operation, not commercial viability, reserve size or acceptable environmental impact.

sources.publisher: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry of Japan
sources.title: Press Conference by Minister Akazawa — successful test mining of rare-earth mud
supports: Japan frames the project as a supply-chain-security initiative
The mud was retrieved from roughly 6,000 metres
Cost reduction and an end-to-end separation/refining process remain unresolved
sources.limitation: Policy statement; does not independently establish economics or environmental performance.

sources.title: Japan identifies large share of rare earths in deep-sea mud off remote island
supports: Reported analysis that approximately 54% of rare-earth content was medium and heavy rare earths
Reported recovery of roughly 50 metric tonnes of mud
Reported target of 350 tonnes per day for the February 2027 trial
visual_evidence_candidates: Reported element list: yttrium, gadolinium and dysprosium
sources.limitation: The Japanese government had not disclosed deposit amount or extent; figures came from limited test sampling and must remain attributed.

sources.title: Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026
supports: Critical-mineral demand continues to grow through 2040
Cobalt demand growth has moderated as LFP battery chemistry expands
Announced and early-stage nickel projects could cover demand in a high-production case
Supply-chain concentration and export restrictions are immediate security risks
Recycling can materially expand but cannot alone eliminate near-term concentration
sources.limitation: Scenario analysis, not a certainty; mineral balances vary by technology, policy and project delivery.

sources.title: Rare Earth Elements — Executive Summary
supports: China accounted for about 60% of magnet rare-earth mining, 91% of refining and 94% of sintered permanent-magnet production in 2024
April 2025 export controls caused sharp export declines and downstream production disruptions
sources.limitation: Figures concern magnet rare earths and related permanent magnets, not all rare-earth elements or all critical minerals.

sources.title: 31st Session of the Council, Part II — 13–24 July 2026
supports: The Council was still working from a further revised consolidated text
An updated list of outstanding issues remained
The final meeting considered remaining work, a roadmap and intersessional work rather than recording an adopted exploitation code
visual_evidence_candidates: July 24 meeting agenda and roadmap language
sources.limitation: Assembly and later intersessional developments must be checked again before narration lock.

sources.title: Exploration Contracts
supports: ISA lists 22 contractors and 32 exploration contracts across nodules, sulphides and cobalt-rich crusts
Chinese entities hold contracts across all three deposit categories
sources.limitation: Exploration contracts are not commercial exploitation approvals.

sources.title: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea — Articles 136 and 137
supports: The seabed beyond national jurisdiction and its resources are described as the common heritage of mankind
States and private actors may not appropriate the Area outside the Convention's framework
sources.limitation: The United States has not ratified UNCLOS and disputes how this regime constrains its nationals; legal interpretation must be attributed.

sources.title: Executive Order 14285 — Unleashing America's Offshore Critical Minerals and Resources
supports: The United States explicitly frames seabed minerals as a national-security and economic priority
The order directs agencies to accelerate exploration, recovery, processing and international partnerships
sources.limitation: Policy direction is not itself a permit or proof of technical/economic feasibility.

sources.title: Deep Seabed Hard Minerals Mining
supports: The United States is not a party to UNCLOS
U.S. law allows exploration licences and commercial recovery permits in areas beyond national jurisdiction subject to DSHMRA review
NOAA finalized a consolidated review rule on 21 January 2026
No DSHMRA commercial recovery permit had yet been issued on the page's current list
sources.limitation: Application and certification status changes quickly and must be rechecked before script lock.

sources.title: The Metals Company Inc. Form 10-Q for quarter ended 31 March 2026
supports: TMC submitted a consolidated exploration and commercial recovery application to NOAA
NOAA's compliance determination was procedural and did not grant or approve the requested licence or permit
sources.limitation: Company filing; resource estimates and timelines remain company statements unless independently verified.

sources.title: Long-term impact and biological recovery in a deep-sea mining track
supports: Visible physical disturbance persisted 44 years after a 1979 collector test
Many biological impacts persisted while some mobile and sediment communities showed recolonization
The test footprint was much smaller and mechanically different from a commercial operation
sources.limitation: Historical small-scale test; not a direct measurement of a future commercial mine.

sources.title: Monitoring benthic plumes, sediment redeposition and seafloor imprints caused by deep-sea polymetallic nodule mining
supports: Collector-generated sediment moved kilometres but remained concentrated near the seabed
Concentrations decreased with time, distance and height
Measured redeposition and erosion provide real physical bounds for plume discussion
sources.limitation: Pre-prototype trial and monitoring geometry do not fully represent long-duration commercial operations.

sources.title: Impacts of an industrial deep-sea mining trial on macrofaunal biodiversity
supports: A 2022 trial recovered more than 3,000 tonnes of nodules
Macrofaunal density fell 37% and species richness fell 32% inside mining tracks two months after disturbance
Plume-affected areas showed altered species-dominance relationships even where abundance change was not detected
sources.limitation: Short post-impact window; does not establish long-term trajectory or full commercial scale.

sources.title: Deep-sea mining discharge can disrupt midwater food webs
supports: Proposed discharge particles are nutritionally poor relative to natural particles
Food-web structure indicates a plausible pathway for disruption among particle feeders and predators
sources.limitation: Demonstrates potential based on food-web and particle analyses, not observed ecosystem collapse from commercial discharge.

sources.title: Lifecycle
supports: The industry's strongest case: nodules may avoid some land disturbance, mine waste and selected lifecycle emissions
Onshore processing assumptions are central to claimed advantages
sources.limitation: Company-commissioned and advocacy framing. Must be paired with independent science and must not be used to settle biodiversity comparisons.
